\chapter{Bread, Water, and Wine}
\label{ch:pt-bread-water-wine}
\hlchaptermodality{11}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name bread, water and wine in Portuguese and hear the -nh- of vinho as Spanish's ñ.}

Say o pão, a água and o vinho, hold água against French's worn-down eau, and pronounce the palatal -nh- of vinho, already met in amanhã.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[o pão]{o pão — bread, worn down to a hum}

\label{lesson:PT-C11-pao}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{o pão} (\textquotedblleft{}bread\textquotedblright{}) — and Portuguese does to it exactly what it did to \textquotedblleft{}father.\textquotedblright{} Just as \emph{pater} eroded to the one-syllable \textbf{pai}, Latin \emph{pānis} wore down to the single \textbf{nasal} syllable \textbf{pão} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{powng}\textquotedblright{}). Same word as French \emph{pain} and Italian \emph{pane}, taken furthest.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{o pão} (\textquotedblleft{}bread\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{pānis}. The intervocalic \emph{-n-} dissolved and left its \textbf{nasality} behind on the vowel: \emph{pānis $\to$ pãe $\to$ pão}, the tilde marking the hum — the identical process behind \textbf{pai} ($\leftarrow$ \emph{pater}) and \textbf{mãe} ($\leftarrow$ \emph{māter}) from the family chapter. Masculine: \emph{o} pão; the plural is the tricky \textbf{pães}.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
Even worn to a hum, the root keeps its English relatives: \textbf{companion / company} (\emph{com-} + \emph{pānis}, \textquotedblleft{}one you \textbf{share bread with}\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{pantry}, \textbf{pannier}. So \emph{pão} and \emph{companion} are the near-vanished and the well-preserved ends of one Latin word.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}o pão\textquotedblright{} — fully nasal, \textquotedblleft{}powng\textquotedblright{}; plural \textquotedblleft{}pães\textquotedblright{}
  \item the parallel — \textquotedblleft{}\emph{pater} $\to$ \textbf{pai}, \emph{pānis} $\to$ \textbf{pão} — same nasal erosion\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pão $\to$ companion, pantry\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give \textquotedblleft{}bread\textquotedblright{} with its article. (\textbf{o pão}.) What Latin word is it from, and what happened to it? (\emph{pānis} — worn to a single \textbf{nasal} syllable, \emph{pānis $\to$ pão}.) Which family word followed the \emph{same} erosion? (\textbf{pai}, $\leftarrow$ \emph{pater} — and \emph{mãe} $\leftarrow$ \emph{māter}.) Next: \textbf{a água} and \textbf{o vinho} — water and wine.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[a água, o vinho]{a água, o vinho — water and wine}

\label{lesson:PT-C11-agua-vinho}



\begin{quote}
Two drinks, two more sound-stories. Portuguese kept \textbf{água} close to Latin \emph{aqua} (unlike French, which dissolved it to \emph{eau}), and it stamps \textbf{vinho} with its signature spelling — the \textbf{-nh-}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{a água} (\textquotedblleft{}water\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{aqua}. Portuguese held its body — \emph{aqua $\to$ água} — where French wore it down to a single vowel (\emph{eau}). The accent on \textbf{á} marks the stress. It's \textbf{feminine}: \emph{a} água. English kept the loud original in \textbf{aquatic, aquarium, aqueduct}.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{o vinho} (\textquotedblleft{}wine\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{vīnum}. The \textbf{-nh-} is Portuguese's palatal \emph{ny} sound — the \textbf{same sound} as Spanish \textbf{ñ} (\emph{viño}$\to$\emph{vinho}), French/Italian \textbf{gn}, and the \emph{nh} you already met in \emph{amanhã} (\textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}). One sound, four spellings across the sisters. The word still gives English \textbf{wine, vine, vinegar, vintage}. Masculine: \emph{o} vinho.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}a água, o vinho\textquotedblright{} — stress the \emph{á}; \emph{-nh-} = palatal \emph{ny}
  \item the contrast — \textquotedblleft{}\emph{aqua} $\to$ \textbf{água} (kept), French \textbf{eau} (worn away)\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}the \emph{nh} of \emph{vinho} = Spanish \emph{ñ}, met before in \emph{amanhã}\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

How does \emph{água} compare with French \emph{eau}, from the same \emph{aqua}? (Portuguese \textbf{kept} the body; French wore it to a vowel.) What sound is the \textbf{-nh-} in \emph{vinho}, and its Spanish twin? (A palatal \emph{ny} — Spanish \textbf{ñ}.) Next chapter: asking for these at a table.
